context.text: Fifty days after Pascha and ten days after the Ascension, the apostles remained in Jerusalem as they had been commanded, gathered in prayer with the Theotokos and the wider company of disciples — about a hundred and twenty persons, as the Acts of the Apostles records. Jerusalem itself was crowded with pilgrims: Pentecost (Shavuot) was one of the three great pilgrim feasts of Israel, celebrating the giving of the Law at Sinai.

narrative.text: On the morning of the feast, Acts records, there came suddenly a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and there appeared divided tongues as of fire, resting on each of them; and all were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues. The gathered pilgrims — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, dwellers in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Rome, Crete, and Arabia — each heard the mighty works of God declared in his own language.

Peter, standing with the eleven, preached the first public sermon of the Church: that Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and raised, is both Lord and Christ, and that the promise of the prophet Joel — 'I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh' — was fulfilled that day. Those who received his word were baptized, 'and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.'

The chapter closes with the first portrait of Church life: the baptized continued steadfastly in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in the prayers — the pattern of doctrine, communion, Eucharist, and liturgical prayer that Orthodoxy recognizes as its own unbroken inheritance.

significance.text: Orthodox tradition calls Pentecost the birthday of the Church, and reads the miracle of tongues as the healing of Babel: where the nations were once scattered into mutual incomprehension, the Spirit now gathers them into one Body without erasing their languages. The feast is also the Church's great trinitarian feast — the kontakion and the icon of Pentecost present the descent of the Spirit as the revelation of the Holy Trinity's saving work: the Father sends the Spirit through the risen Son.

Every Orthodox ordination, chrismation, and epiclesis stands in continuity with this day: the Church does not merely remember Pentecost but lives from it, asking the Father at every Liturgy to send down the same Spirit 'upon us and upon these gifts here offered.'

consequences.text: From this gathering the mission of the Church unfolds exactly along the line the risen Christ had traced — Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth. The council held at Jerusalem some fifteen years later, and the missionary journeys of Paul, are the direct continuation of what began at Pentecost.

uncertainty: The event is dated by tradition to the Pentecost following the Crucifixion, conventionally placed at AD 33 (some chronologies prefer AD 30). The year shown here is the conventional traditional date, not a documented civil date.
